meta.title: No, local models will not win
meta.author: liberty

comments.author: liberty
comments.text:
For me, local, open-source (not "open weight") models are the only things that would cause me to consider using LLMs. If there isn't an endpoint in which we're not renting our brains instead of using them ourselves, what's the point even for those who are enthusiastic about LLMs?

I disagree with the author about LLMs in general, but I agree with the conclusion. If the one people can rent is better, they're more likely to want to use that. There doesn't appear to be a positive end result for users and programmers without the market otherwise crashing.

comments.author: mdaniel
comments.text:
For me, local, open-source


Just for my curiosity, do you consider that list to be models that are declared open source, ones that are open-source + open-data, or you really mean you will only use ones that you have trained yourself?

I ask because I have a standing rule that I don't consider software to be truly open source unless I can build it, because a code dump is not the same as my ability to affect change to that codebase. But, very similar to Chromium, if it is so incredibly compute intensive to do so that I need to rent a m500.xxgargantuan, that's really skating the line for me. I literally cannot possibly imagine how much local horsepower would be required to replicate (e.g.) TildeAI's allegedly open model

comments.author: liberty
comments.text:
Technically, I'd allow it. It'd be far better than the status quo especially if all the other problems with LLMs were resolved. Reproducible builds would be nice here but since LLM training is probabilistic I'm not sure how it could apply here.

That said, I've compiled Chromium on a mid tier laptop. It took like 12 hours. We're talking a whole other beast here.

I guess an important question is at what level LLMs are best modified. If it's pretraining, then yeah they need to be trained on my laptop to be useful. But if they're more like game assets where they are more useful in combination with other software and can be tweaked afterwards with other tools, I'm more okay with not necessarily being able to train one myself.

I'm concerned about potential AI apocalypse scenarios (including "AI doesn't take over everything but ownership of AI becomes increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few trillionaires and everyone else is forced into subsistence" as well as mass surveillance), but I don't find the "renting our brains" argument to be very persuasive.

comments.author: mempko
comments.text:
Cost is not always the consideration people use for deciding what model to use. If cost was a huge factor Anthropic wouldn't be dominating OpenAI right now since it's by far the most expensive solution to rent.

The biggest reason to use local models is autonomy and robustness, not efficiency. If you need a model to always be there, local is great. If you want a model to not change under you as you use it then local is great. If you want control over when to update your model, then local is great. Also if you want to experiment with new ways of using a model (for example, novel structured output) or fine-tuning then local is great.

The future in the medium term will be hybrid. Look at Apple and Google. They run some stuff on phones and others on the server.

comments.author: abareplace
comments.text: In some cases, you can also choose a local model due to privacy concerns. If all inference were done by huge corporations, it would put too much power in their hands and make them vulnerable to insider attacks.

comments.author: mdaniel
comments.text:
of course it's software - that's why the repos carry their own license and have innovations in the architecture of how machine learning primitives are glued together in novel ways

put another way: if you download https://huggingface.co/google/bert_uncased_L-2_H-128_A-2/blob/main/model.safetensors it's not going to do you any good since they are just a ton of floating point numbers. Do you know what (ahem) transforms the numbers into some outcome? software

that's also why this directory only grows over time, because each one of the special little snowflakes needs their own special little concessions to know how to do something with those weights https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/v5.15.0/src/transformers/models

comments.author: laurentbroy
comments.text:
There is this classic book, The Innovator Dilemma that describes decades of worse technology beating "better" ones.

The TL;DR of that book: newer, "worse" technology always hit a point were they are good enough for the use cases of their users. When that inflection point occurs, the differentiator start being on other dimensions (cost being a frequent one), and the newer, "worse" technology, now good enough for the older technology users, start being appealing for the benefit along these new dimensions, and the mass of users start abandoning the older, "better" technology, even though it still perform vastly better along the previous dimension.

See:


Flash storage vs Harddrive (Harddrive still contains more data, but flash is faster)

PC vs MiniComputer vs Mainframe

LCD vs CRT (LCD used to have terrible images, but they were the only options for laptops, then they became good enough for desktop computer. Graphic Designer moved last.)

Digital Photography vs Film (they still shoot movie on film)

DSLR vs Phone Camera (DSLR take better picture, but Phone Camera are more than good enough for family picture)

Open Source vs Proprietary Database (MySQL in the LAMP stack won the website market despite spotty transaction and foreign key support )


The interesting point is that it is a gradual process and it is often the low paying users that leave first, leaving the impression for the legacy technology firm that margins are improving. Those firms move upmarket, serve higher paying customer that need the legacy technology better performance. But at some point, even for the higher paying customer, the newer technology start being good enough. And since that newer technology was built of smaller margin and price points, it is vastly cheaper. The high paying customers move on to reduce costs, and the legacy firm completely collapse.

The "Local models are not useless" section kind of address this, but fail to point out that at some point in the future, local model may jump out of their niche and kill the frontier model business. It doesn't matter if frontier models are better in the absolute. It matter that they are good enough in a way that local model are not.

comments.author: carlana
comments.text:
If you go back far enough, a printed book is clearly worse than an illuminated manuscript. Gutenberg gave up on rubricating (writing words in red) with type because it was too much hassle to do a second pass, so he just had it handwritten after the fact. It still cut down costs by so much compared to handwriting the whole thing, it didn't matter that you don't get neat little illustrations of cats or snails or whatever. :-)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible#Rubrication,_illumination_and_binding

comments.author: frontsideair
comments.text:
almost everyone’s revealed preference is to use the strongest available model in their price range


That is true for now, but once we hit diminishing returns it may change. At work, I do not use Fable, or even Opus sometimes, because they have become so similar in terms of capabilities. And providers also have to make the models even more proactive to get over the diminishing returns, which I don't prefer personally. For personal projects. Qwen3.6 27B is enough for most of my needs.


datacenter models are always going to be cheaper


That's a weak reason, I prefer local models because of data privacy mainly. I also like that I will always have access to it, and it works offline. And my GPU is both for gaming and inference, so it's not single purpose.

In the end, as they keep building more datacenters, local models may not "win" but that win condition is a false one. Local models don't have to be better or fully phase out cloud models. I think they are already good and cheap enough, and they'll only get better at closing the gap.

comments.author: frontsideair
comments.text:

comments.author: gerikson
comments.text:
Stuff moves so fast, it's easy to forget how just a short time ago, ChatGPT was the most downloaded app on mobile app stores, and people were confidently predicted that more people would pay OpenAI monthly than were paying Netflix.

This narrative has quietly died down, as focus has shifted towards "agentic workflows" in software development. But just as consumers are gonna look at a monthly $20 bill for ChatGPT and say "nah, it's not worth it", companies can take a look at their monthly token spend, check what they're getting for it, and decide it's too much.

Economics is like physics - it can look like you're defying gravity on the top of a parabola, but gravity and money people actually have available to spend always wins.

comments.author: frontsideair
comments.text: Very well put. They made a daily usable model with GPT 3.5 and now they are moving the goalposts for themselves for agentic, long-horizon enterprise use cases in hopes of turning a profit, but that may not even pan out due to token costs. I guess their next goal is cybersecurity arms race, which is absolutely abhorrent but what else could we expect? Casual users are nowhere in the equation.

comments.author: mdaniel

If that were true, no one would have a general purpose computer because the cloud is better, or Amazon Luna or GeForce Now would replace gaming rigs, etc

almost everyone’s revealed preference is to use the strongest available model in their price range.

comments.author: mordae
comments.text:
Current MoE (DeepSeek) are already shuttling pretty thin slices of expert weights per token while keeping the context processing and shared expert busy.

This split, i.e. hot dense rasoning loop slowly fed relevant knowledge, might be a local optimum for inference at the edge.

Fast 32GiB VRAM GPU on 64GB/s PCIe fed from 128GiB RAM is currently (ignoring RAMpocalypse) higher mid-end workstation. Would load prompt in 2s (give or take) and generate at 50 tokens/second with MTP.

That is fully sufficient for office work, coding assistance and research. Yes, you need to retrain the model every couple of months for it to keep up, but the architecture is bounded by the physics of the available hardware.

The same hardware arrangement is required for realistic gaming, so unless Steam is going under, replaced by consoles, the hardware is not going away.

And one might argue it will take exactly one high profile case of cloud provider leaking internal company data to a competitor to create serious demand for edge inference in the corporate world.

comments.author: thesnarky1
comments.text:
And one might argue it will take exactly one high profile case of cloud provider leaking internal company data to a competitor to create serious demand for edge inference in the corporate world.


I think it would take less than that. I firmly believe the business resiliency issue will be a bigger one since that has a much more immediate response. Just look at the Hugging Face lessons learned: don't count on an external model when you need to rely on the answer.

The day Open AI or Anthropic turn off for some number of hours, every business that has integrated their operations with those providers is going to immediately look for a way to host their own model at a minimum as a hedge against the risk, potentially as a replacement for the risk.

comments.author: sardaukar
comments.text: I can emulate a PS2 on a 50$ handheld these days. Current models will be available locally in 5 years time, and they'll be the 700$ HP laptop - more than enough for most people.

comments.author: ache
comments.text:
It's not my conclusion.

For me local models does everything a bigger model could do, because I don't have extraordinary use cases. AgentWorld / Ortnith-1.0 are very good at prototyping (source code), Gemma is quick to act as a "Classifier". I don't need more. Local models may soon run on a potato and be good enough for everyone while big models are staging currently.

Never a 3T model will be outsmarted by a 30B model, but if 80% of the 3T model tasks are done by the 30B, what is the use case for the 3T model? Does the 20% tasks justify all the infrastructure and environmental costs?

I refuse to pay any cent to any LLM provider.

If I pay a model, it must be open-source, fully open-source.

I wouldn't discount that this might be a model that some people want to work with and could be economically good enough.

comments.author: erock
comments.text:
It's pretty clear that one GPU per developer with a local model is not going to be likely.


This is not clear at all.  I use qwen3.6 27b (on consumer 24gb vram hardware) with great success.  I think particularly for coding agents smaller models might have a chance to win especially when scaling LLMs stalls.  Even if they are simply used for read-only + debugging it can be incredibly useful.

comments.author: elliotmorris
comments.text:
In a year you might be able to run something about as strong as GPT-5.6-Sol on your laptop. But by then, you’ll think of GPT-5.6-Sol as too weak to be useful.



...



When given a choice, people are going to pick the model that frustrates them less, which is always going to be the bigger, more powerful one.


I still think Opus 4.5 is about as useful as these things ever got for me. That was 9 months or so ago. I would still choose it if available. When I remember to check, I always pick the furthest back Opus model.

I'm not sure you can trust revealed preference here, people are not really making a choice, they're just pressing go. User behavior will dramatically shift if cost becomes a more prevalent factor in day to day model use, as it almost certainly must.

In fact, I think there's something to be said that larger more powerful models become less appropriate for certain tasks. It's hard to know with all the "effort" stuff that's in play now, but it's sometimes difficult to get the latest models to stop thinking and just do the thing.

comments.author: kafka
comments.text:
This article completely ignores privacy, which doesn't make sense to me. There are several use-cases for LLMs that only really work when the model runs locally. It seems like the public in general doesn't care about this as much as they once did (maybe they never cared?), so I don't think this affects everyone. But me personally, the few workflows that I see myself wanting to do in the future (I don't use LLM much outside of work) have the hard requirement of privacy since they involve my personal data

There's also a lot of assumptions in the article, to the point that it reads as not only pro-AI, but AI-backed

comments.author: plop
comments.text:
If I had a capable GPU I'd be trying open models a lot more.

I think we're going to get small models for specialised tasks like NER.

comments.author: afogel
comments.text: I'm not convinced by the author's claim -- I think the the world model of local models as an all-purpose model may not win against large, hosted, frontier models, but as a specialized task reasoners, I think we're seeing increasing evidence that they can be deployed highly effectively.
